title: Tables, code and figures
summary: Tables, code and figures break text splitters. Keep each as a unit, repeat headers and signatures, and turn figures into searchable descriptions linked to the original image.
useIf: Documents carry tables, code or diagrams and users ask about the values, functions or pictures inside them.
avoidIf: The corpus is prose only. Do not pay for table, code and figure handling you will never retrieve.

explain.md: A splitter that counts tokens treats a table as a stream of words. Cut it mid-row and the numbers are no longer attached to their column headers. Code split at a token limit separates a function body from its signature. A figure is not text at all unless you create text for it. The fix is to detect these elements during parsing and give each a **chunking rule of its own**.

explain.md: Parsing supplies the structure. Document Intelligence layout v4.0 returns Markdown with HTML tables, handwriting flags and figure regions [[tr41]]. The Content Understanding skill in AI Search outputs tables and figures as Markdown; its AI image descriptions are an opt-in preview in `2026-05-01-preview` (checked 2026-10-13) [[tr5]]. The Azure Architecture Center warns that if an image description is split across chunks, the image URL should be repeated in each chunk, and shows an analyzer that adds title, summary and keywords as metadata [[tr9]].

explain.title: Numbers need exact terms
explain.md: Dense embeddings are weak at exact numbers and identifiers (practice). For table-heavy corpora pair vector search with keyword search, and consider adding a short text summary of each table next to it so natural-language questions also match.

blocks.md: Parse code into functions, methods and classes with a syntax-aware splitter, then store each with its file path, signature and docstring. A short header such as `src/billing/tax.py :: compute_vat(amount, region)` makes the chunk findable by name and by purpose. Very long functions can be split at inner blocks with the signature repeated.

Create a text chunk per meaningful figure: caption, nearby sentence and a generated description of what the chart or diagram shows, plus page and image URL for display. Skip decorative images. A vision model adds cost per image, so classify first and describe only figures that carry information.

whereToUse: Financial statements, spec sheets and pricing tables where users ask for specific values
Engineering knowledge bases mixing prose, diagrams and code samples
Slide decks and reports where charts carry the key message
Any corpus parsed by a layout model that already identifies tables and figures

use: Questions are about values in tables, functions in code or content of charts
A parser exposes tables and figures as separate elements
You can store the image or table source for display
avoid: Decorative images that carry no information
No parser capable of recognising tables, so the extra rules would run on garbled text
flips: Tables are huge: chunk by row groups with repeated headers and add a summary
Numbers dominate questions: add keyword or structured lookup beside vectors
Image volume is high: describe only classified informative figures

pitfalls.symptom: The assistant quotes the wrong year's figure
pitfalls.cause: A large table was split and later chunks lost the header row, so values lack their column labels
pitfalls.fix: Repeat the header row in every row-group chunk and include the caption

pitfalls.symptom: Searching a function name finds nothing
pitfalls.cause: Code was split by tokens, so the signature is in a different chunk or the name is absent
pitfalls.fix: Chunk by symbol and prepend path and signature to each chunk

pitfalls.symptom: A figure description is retrieved but the image link is missing
pitfalls.cause: The description was split across chunks and only one carries the URL
pitfalls.fix: Repeat the image URL in each chunk of the description, as the Architecture Center advises

pitfalls.symptom: Parsing code that read checkbox tokens breaks after an upgrade
pitfalls.cause: Document Intelligence v4.0 `2024-11-30` returns tables as HTML and checkboxes as ☒ and ☐
pitfalls.fix: Pin the API version and keep a parsing regression set

scenarios.title: Financial tables with comparison questions
scenarios.situation: Analysts ask for values and year-over-year comparisons from long financial statements. Tables run to many rows and columns. Keyword search also exists.
unknowns: Do questions compare rows, columns or both?
How long is the longest table?
scenarios.question: How do you chunk the tables?

options.name: Row-group chunks with the header row and caption repeated, plus a short text summary per table
options.why: Values stay attached to column labels, comparisons within a group work and the summary helps natural-language matching.
options.tradeoff: Repeated headers add tokens and the summary needs generation.

options.name: One row per chunk in key: value form
options.tradeoff: Comparisons across rows need several chunks and lose layout.

options.name: Flatten tables to plain text and chunk at 512 tokens
options.why: Numbers drift away from their headers when chunks are cut.
options.tradeoff: Fine only when tables are minor and the answers lie in prose.

flips.if: Every row is an independent record such as a product
flips.then: One row per chunk becomes best.

scenarios.takeaway: Keep values attached to their headers in every chunk.

scenarios.title: Engineering docs with diagrams and code
scenarios.situation: An engineering portal mixes prose, architecture diagrams and code samples. Users ask how a component works and where a function lives. Image volume is high and many images are logos or icons.
constraints: Code samples are searchable by name
unknowns: What share of images are informative?
scenarios.question: What is your plan?

options.name: Chunk code by symbol with path and signature, and describe only informative figures with caption, description and image URL
options.why: Functions are found by name, diagrams become searchable and vision spend goes only where information lives.
options.tradeoff: A classifier step and some missed borderline images.

options.name: Ignore figures and index text and code only
options.why: Cheapest, and captions may carry some meaning.
options.tradeoff: Answers that depend on a diagram are missing.

options.name: Describe every image with a vision model
options.why: Pays for logos and icons, and noisy descriptions pollute results.
options.tradeoff: Right for scanned slides where every image is content.

flips.if: Most images turn out to be informative charts
flips.then: Describe them all and budget for it.
Use captions as the description and skip the vision call.

scenarios.takeaway: Spend parsing and vision budget only on elements users will retrieve.

quiz.q: The assistant gives the right row's value but the wrong year. The table was split into several chunks. Most likely cause?
options: Later chunks lack the header row, so values have no column labels
The embedding dimension is too small
quiz.explain: Chunks after the first have values without headers, so the year column is lost. Overlap, dimensions and index type are not the cause of this symptom.

quiz.q: Match each content type to a good chunk unit.

pairs.r: One row per chunk, as key: value pairs
Row groups with the header repeated
One function or class with path and signature
A text description chunk with the image URL

quiz.explain: Each unit keeps meaning intact: records, headers, symbols and descriptions. A fixed token window would separate values from headers and signatures from bodies.

quiz.q: Which are sound ways to reduce vision-model cost for figures?
options: Classify images and describe only informative ones
Reuse captions as descriptions when they are rich
Describe every decorative icon for completeness
Skip all figures even when charts hold the answers
quiz.explain: Classification and caption reuse save calls without losing key content. Describing icons wastes spend and adds noise, and skipping everything loses answers that live in charts.

flashcards.front: How do you chunk a table that is too large for one chunk?
flashcards.back: Split by row groups and repeat the header row and caption in every chunk so values keep their column labels.
By symbol (function, method, class), with file path and signature attached, instead of at a fixed token limit.

flashcards.front: What does the Azure Architecture Center say about split image descriptions?
flashcards.back: If a description is split across chunks, repeat the image URL in each chunk so every hit can show the image.
